message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review is grounded in two months of actual till data for every main course, a full competitor price check, and the latest supplier information, so the recommendations are not guesswork. The price increases are modest and targeted: each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices for that dish, so we remain the value option in the area, and with 60% of bookings from repeat guests our customer base is loyal enough to absorb a pound or two. The projected effect is simple to check, £810 a week or about £42,000 a year in additional gross profit, which lifts our main-course margin to about 71%. I also think the menu-mix decision is clear-cut: the data show the mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so replacing it with a seasonal special is an easy improvement. Monitoring for eight weeks gives us an early warning if volumes move. Overall I believe these changes are sensible, low-risk and well evidenced.
</author>

<document>
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
</document>
response:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

**Verdict:** The data and arithmetic are mostly sound, and the price rises themselves look reasonable against competitors. But the paper has two significant problems:
- it ignores the **12% beef cost rise** it reports, which takes a large share of the projected gain;
- the **case for removing the risotto is backwards**. It has the *highest* margin on the menu, not the weakest.

There is also a possible VAT issue that could overstate every margin and profit figure.

## 1. The risotto has the best margin, not the weakest
Table 1 shows the mushroom risotto at **80%, the highest margin of any main**. It also earns more gross profit per plate (£11.20) than the burger (£10.80) or the curry (£10.90). Its sales of 90 plates a week are the lowest, but tied with specials.

Replacing it with a seasonal special at the same price would probably **reduce** profit. Specials run at 64%. At £14, a 64% special earns about £8.96 a plate against the risotto's £11.20, a loss of roughly **£200 a week** on current volumes.

If the risotto is the only vegetarian main, removing it also risks losing whole tables where one guest is vegetarian. The paper should either drop proposal 5.2, or justify it on grounds other than margin, such as freshness or menu variety.

## 2. The beef price rise isn't in the projection
Section 4 reports a **12% beef price rise from 1 April**, the same day the new prices start, but Section 5.3 ignores it. As an upper bound, applying 12% to the whole food cost of beef dishes:

| | Extra cost per plate | Plates/week | Extra cost/week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Burger (£4.20 food cost) | £0.50 | 260 | £131 |
| Sirloin (£10.40 food cost) | £1.25 | 120 | £150 |
| **Total** | | | **≈ £281** |

- **Net gain falls from £810 to about £530 a week,** roughly **£27,500 a year** rather than £42,000. The real figure lies somewhere between, depending on how much of each plate's cost is beef.
- **Most of the steak increase is absorbed.** The £2 rise gains only about 75p a plate after the cost rise.
- **Main-course margin barely moves.** On the five priced dishes, margin is about 69.9% now. It reaches about 71.3% after the price rises *without* the beef increase, but only about **69.7% with it**. The claim that margins rise to 71% doesn't hold.

## 3. Check whether the margins include VAT
UK menu prices must include VAT, and gross margin is normally calculated on the net price. The table's margins appear to use VAT-inclusive prices. For example, fish and chips shows 69% on £16.50. On a net price of £13.75, the margin is about **63%**.

The same applies to the projection. Each £1 rise is about **83p** of extra revenue after VAT, so the £810 a week would be about **£675** before even allowing for beef. If the figures already exclude VAT, add a footnote saying so. If they don't, recalculate the margins, the projection and the comparison with the 70% target.

## 4. Other points
- **Trading days.** Section 2 says the restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday, which is **five** days. The recommendation says "six trading days."
- **The margin problem may lie elsewhere.** Mains already run at about 70% on the table's own basis, while the *overall* food margin has fallen to 67%. Starters, desserts or specials may be the bigger drag. A paper that only reprices mains may not restore the overall target.
- **The monitoring baseline is seasonal.** Comparing spring trade against January and February, usually the quietest months, will probably show volumes *rising* whatever the effect of the price change. Compare against the same weeks last year, or track the share of each dish in the overall mix.
- **Assuming volumes hold.** The paper offers no evidence for this beyond the 2024 increase. A simple sensitivity test would help. For example, how much volume could fish and chips lose before the rise stops paying for itself?
- **Repeat guests.** The 60% repeat base supports loyalty, but those guests are also the most likely to notice the increases. That's a reason to keep the rises modest, which they are, rather than a reason to expect no reaction.

## 5. What holds up
- The margin calculations in Table 1, on the basis used.
- The plate count: the dishes sum to 1,050 a week.
- The competitor check. All three new prices sit below the midpoint of each competitor range (£17.98, £16.50 and £29.50).
- The arithmetic of the £810 a week and £42,120 a year before costs.
- The weekly monitoring plan, with a better baseline.

## Recommended changes
1. Withdraw or rewrite the risotto proposal. Its margin is the highest on the menu.
2. Include the 12% beef rise in the projection. The net gain is about £27,500–42,000 a year rather than £42,000, and main-course margin stays at about 70%.
3. Confirm whether the margins exclude VAT, and recalculate them if not.
4. Correct "six trading days" to five.
5. Look at whether starters, desserts or specials explain the drop in overall margin.
6. Use a same-season baseline for monitoring, and add a simple volume sensitivity test.
7. Update the cover note. Its claims that the risotto has the weakest margin, that profit rises by £42,000, and that margin reaches 71% need revising.
